power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p=0.14", Sentence = "It was lower in adenomyosis patients, but the difference was not statistically significant (p=0.14, Fig. 4G)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. text.text: Capsule: The myometrium of adenomyosis patients present a significantly lower amount of muscle-relaxing, adrenergic nerve fibers.
We explain how this underpins junctional zone thickening and dyscontractility in this pathology.
The myometrium is the thickest smooth muscle (SM) of the human body: ~2.5 cm in the nonpregnant female.
Its menstrual-cycle-dependent peristaltic contractions (De Ziegler et al., 2001) play a major role in sperm propulsion at ovulation (Kunz et al., 1996) and in menses evacuation (Lyons et al., 1991).
text.formatted: Its menstrual-cycle-dependent peristaltic contractions <ref type="bibr">(De Ziegler et al., 2001)</ref> play a major role in sperm propulsion at ovulation <ref type="bibr">(Kunz et al., 1996)</ref> and in menses evacuation <ref type="bibr">(Lyons et al., 1991)</ref>.

text.text: While contraction of the full thickness of the myometrium is required for parturition, only the inner myometrium participates in peristaltic activity of the non-pregnant uterus (1) (2) (3).
text.formatted: While contraction of the full thickness of the myometrium is required for parturition, only the inner myometrium participates in peristaltic activity of the non-pregnant uterus <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3)</ref>.

text.text: This implies that the outer myometrium is actively maintained in a quiescent state outside of pregnancy.
In endometriosis patients, intra-uterine pressure, contraction frequency and amplitude are elevated by a factor 2-3 compared to healthy women (Bulletti et al., 2002).
text.formatted: In endometriosis patients, intra-uterine pressure, contraction frequency and amplitude are elevated by a factor 2-3 compared to healthy women <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Bulletti et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: This hypercontractility likely plays a causal role in disease emergence, by favoring chronic retrograde transport of menstrual debris to the abdominal cavity (Kunz et al., 2005; Sampson, 1927; Vercellini et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This hypercontractility likely plays a causal role in disease emergence, by favoring chronic retrograde transport of menstrual debris to the abdominal cavity <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Kunz et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Sampson, 1927;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Vercellini et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Adenomyosis is characterized by the invasion of endometrium inside the myometrium (4).
text.formatted: Adenomyosis is characterized by the invasion of endometrium inside the myometrium <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4)</ref>.

text.text: Poor myometrial contraction coordination has recently been reported in women suffering from this pathology (Rees et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Poor myometrial contraction coordination has recently been reported in women suffering from this pathology <ref type="bibr">(Rees et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: A thickened junctional zone (JZ >12 mm) on MRI is 85-93% specific of adenomyosis (5, 6).
text.formatted: A thickened junctional zone (JZ >12 mm) on MRI is 85-93% specific of adenomyosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6)</ref>.

text.text: JZ thickening is also found in 79% of endometriosis patients (7).
text.formatted: JZ thickening is also found in 79% of endometriosis patients <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref>.

text.text: The reasons underlying JZ thickening and dyscontractility in endometriosis and adenomyosis remain unknown.

text.text: We therefore use here modern technics of mosaic epifluorescence imaging combined with machine-learning assisted segmentation to quantitatively characterize the cellular organization of the full-thickness myometrium and its alterations in adenomyosis.
We present serosa-to-endometrium density profiles of smooth muscle, vasculature, general innervation (PGP9.5), and sympathetic adrenergic innervation (TH) in control and adenomyosis patients.
We also harness label-free second harmonic generation imaging (SHG) (19, 20) to quantify collagen I & III fibers; this powerful tool has only recently been introduced in the field of gynecology (21).

text.text: We uncover a sharp depletion of adrenergic muscle-relaxing nerve fibers in the inner myometrium of adenomyosis patients compared to control patients.
This finding rationalizes uterine dyscontractility and JZ thickening in adenomyosis.

text.text: Approval for this study was granted under IRB number 00012157 from the Groupe Ethique Recherche Médicale (GERM) of Hôpital Paris Saint Joseph.
All women were provided with written information about the study and consented to participate.
After surgery, the uterus was opened by sectioning the anterior wall along the cervix-to-fundus axis.

A ~25x10x10 mm block of myometrium, from serosa to endometrium, was cut out from the anterior uterine wall, at a position halfway between cervix and fundus, avoiding, when present, any visible myomas.
The tissue block was immediately fixed in 4% PFA overnight, at 4°C. It was then washed 3x1 hour in PBS, and kept in PBS with 0.02% sodium azide at 4°C until sections were performed.
The tissue block was dehydrated in 30% sucrose solution for 24h and embedded in PolyFreeze (Sigma).
Biopsies were oriented in a way that the presumably serosal longitudinal SM fibers (22, 23) were in the section plane, and that presumably circular fibers were perpendicular to the section plane.

text.text: Some samples where orientation was lost or unknown were not included in the SM fiber orientation analysis. 18 µm-thick sections were cut on a cryotome (Leica) and adhered on SuperFrost glass slides.
Permeabilization and blocking were performed in PBS + 1% bovine serum albumin (Fraction V, Sigma) + triton 0.1% for 1 hour.

Slides were incubated with the following antibodies overnight: αSMA Cy3-conjugated (Sigma C6198, 1:1000), PECAM AF647-conjugated (SCBT sc-376764, 1:100), rabbit anti-PGP9.5 (Abcam AB108986, 1:100) or rabbit anti-TH (Abcam AB112, 1:100).
When a secondary antibody was necessary (PGP9.5, TH), we washed the slide 3x10 min in PBS and then applied anti-rabbit Cy3 secondary (Thermofisher, 1:500) for 2 h.
All steps were performed at RT, under constant, gentle agitation to optimize staining homogeneity.
All slides were finally washed in PBS, coverslipped, and imaged.

Imaging was performed at the ImagoSeine microscopy platform on an inverted Zeiss wide-field epifluorescence microscope, at x10 magnification, by mosaic-stitching of ~100-300 tiles, depending on sample size.

Acquisition settings were kept constant for all samples in order for collagen densities to be quantitatively compared.
For each staining, a new model was trained until the segmented image visually matched the distribution of the labeled cells.
The segmented binary was exported and its profile measured along a curvilinear line, 1 to 5 mm thick, from serosa to endometrium.

The result was converted in % area density, all profiles were subsampled to 1000 points ranging from 0 (serosa) to 1 (SM-endometrium junction) and average curves for each patient group produced under Matlab.

text.text: We have recently shown that the myometrium has a uniform organ-bath contractility (33) : IM and OM have similar ex vivo contraction amplitude and frequency.
Because nerve connections have been severed during the hysterectomy operation, these ex vivo experiments reveal a uniform, spontaneous myogenic contractility.
When contractility is observed in-vivo by TVUS or MRI, only the IM is seen to contract (1-3): contractile waves fade as they enter the OM.

A simple synthetic explanation of these results is that activity of the myometrium results from: 1°) a uniform, spontaneous myogenic contractility, 2°) a nerve-mediated adrenergic inhibition of this myogenic contractility in the OM.
This combined neuro-muscular activity determines in-fine the thickness of myometrium that is involved in contractile activity of the non-pregnant uterus.
The thickness of tonic SM is precisely the JZ (34, 35).

text.text: TH adrenergic fibers were significantly depleted in the IM of adenomyosis uteri.
This depletion entails that a greater thickness of muscle is involved in the uterine contractile activity of these patients.

This has several functional consequences: 1°) a thicker JZ (34, 35), which is today among the diagnostic criteria of adenomyosis, 2°) higher intra-uterine pressure (36), which is closely related to pain sensation (37, 38), 3°) the involvement of deeper layers of the myometrium, and in particular the spiral and longitudinal layers which can generate bucklingtype deformation of the epithelial lining (39).

text.text: Contraceptive pills are the number one line of treatment in endometriosis and adenomyosis.
Because they reduce the serum concentrations of estrogen by a factor ~10 (50), they should, theoretically, favor adrenergic innervation and consequently reduce uterine hyper-contractility.
Dedicated studies on the effect of the combined pill, of progesterone-only pill, and of pill withdrawal on the adrenergic innervation of the myometrium in animal models would be very beneficial.
The plasticity of sympathetic uterine innervation may offer decisive cues to re-establish normal uterine innervation and contractile activity in patients on the long-term.
We did not have access to patient MRI data, and were thus not able to directly correlate JZ thickness with the extent of TH fiber depletion.
Our argument instead relies on the fact that the JZ is statistically thicker in adenomyosis patients compared to controls.

We also in most cases (34/48) did not know the menstrual cycle phase of the patient at the time of hysterectomy; we however believe that cyclic myometrium architecture changes should be small compared to the vast TH fiber depletion observed in the adenomyosis group.

text.text: Finally, we have investigated here only the average density profiles of various cellular components across the myometrium thickness: local remodeling around adenomyosis lesions will be reported elsewhere.
We examined the density gradients of smooth muscle, blood vessel, collagen and nerve fibers in full thickness myometrium sections.
Our study revealed a drastic depletion of inhibitory, adrenergic nerve fibers in the inner myometrium of adenomyosis patients.
This depletion entails that a thicker layer of uterine muscle is tonic in these women, explaining their characteristically thick JZ.
We hypothesize that the nerve depletion could be due to defective re-innervation of the myometrium post-parturition and/or hyper-estrogenism.

Future investigations may reveal how the intrinsic plasticity of adrenergic innervation could be harnessed to re-establish normal uterine contractile activity in adenomyosis, endometriosis and severe dysmenorrhea.
